opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I get a lot, and the honest answer is that it wasn't one dramatic moment. It was a feeling that built up over a few years.

At Google I was surrounded by incredibly talented people, and the infrastructure was unmatched. You could train models at a scale most of the world couldn't touch. But a lot of that energy was going into products that, while useful, were optimizing things that were already pretty good: a slightly better recommendation, a slightly better ranking. I kept asking myself where this technology would make the biggest difference, not a two percent improvement but a qualitative change in what humans can do.

Science kept coming up as the answer. If you look at how discovery actually happens in biology, chemistry, or materials science, it's still remarkably slow and manual. A PhD student might spend years running experiments that are essentially a search through an enormous space of possibilities, guided by intuition and a bit of luck. That's exactly the kind of problem where machine learning shines: high-dimensional search, pattern recognition, learning from noisy data. We'd started to see glimpses of this. Protein structure prediction was a wake-up call for a lot of us. It showed that AI could crack a problem scientists had worked on for fifty years.

The second piece was more personal. I wanted to work much closer to the full loop, from the model to the wet lab to the actual result, and see whether a prediction holds up in the real world. In a large company you're often one layer removed from that. Doing it in a smaller, more focused setting means you can design the whole system around discovery, including how you generate data, not just how you model it.

And there's a timing element. I felt there was a window, maybe five or ten years, where AI for science would go from interesting papers to something that changes how research is done. I didn't want to watch that happen from the sidelines. So the risk of leaving felt smaller than the regret of not trying.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts incremental product improvements with AI’s potential to transform scientific discovery, but it does not identify a gap between current AI models and AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a single moment. It built up over a few years.

At Google I was working on large models, and the work was fantastic. The infrastructure, the colleagues, the scale of problems you could touch. But I kept noticing that the questions I found most exciting weren't the ones about making a chatbot answer a little better or a search ranking a little sharper. They were the questions on the edges, where a model stumbled onto something that looked like real structure in the physical world.

I have a physics background, and I spent my earlier years in a lab, doing experiments by hand. I remember how slow it was. You'd spend months on a sample, a measurement would fail, and you'd start over. The intuition you built was real, but it was expensive. So when I saw models starting to do things like predict protein structure, or propose candidate materials, or spot patterns in experimental data that a human would miss, something clicked. I thought, this is the thing I actually care about. Not AI as a product, but AI as a new kind of instrument.

The other piece was timing. There's a window right now where the methods are mature enough to be useful, but the science side hasn't fully absorbed them yet. Most labs still work the way they did twenty years ago. That gap felt like an opportunity, and also a responsibility. If people who understand both sides don't step into it, it either gets filled badly or it gets filled slowly.

And frankly, inside a large company, you can push on these problems, but the incentives pull you back toward the core business. That's not a criticism, it's just gravity. I wanted to work somewhere the scientific question itself was the point, where a result that advances a field counts as a win even if it never ships as a feature.

So leaving wasn't about leaving Google. It was about getting closer to the thing that got me into research in the first place.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI’s potential to aid scientific discovery and a gap in labs’ adoption of AI, but does not identify current models’ inadequate scientific innovation capacity as a gap between AI and AGI.

astra-6.text:
What drew me to AI for scientific discovery was the possibility of turning advances in computing into a deeper understanding of the physical world. AI can help us recognize patterns, but the really exciting question is whether it can help us generate hypotheses, design experiments, and discover something we didn’t know before.

I valued my time at Google, but I wanted to make that question the center of my work. In science, a promising prediction is only the beginning—you still have to test it against reality. That connection between building models and doing experiments was what I wanted to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI helping generate hypotheses, design experiments, and make discoveries, but it does not identify inadequate scientific innovation capacity as a gap between current AI models and AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the motivation was the possibility of using AI to help us understand the physical world. There are so many scientific questions where progress is limited by how quickly we can explore ideas, run experiments, and interpret the results. I wanted to work on tools that could accelerate that process.

Leaving Google was an opportunity to focus more directly on that ambition. The question I wanted to pursue was: can AI help scientists discover something they otherwise wouldn’t have found?

r001.rationale: The response describes scientific progress being limited by the pace of exploration, experiments, and interpretation, but does not identify inadequate scientific innovation as a gap between current AI models and AGI.
